message.content:
Here’s a mix of classic, modern, and cult‑favorite horror films you might enjoy:

| Year | Title | Why it’s worth watching |
|------|-------|------------------------|
| 1960 | **Psycho** (dir. Alfred Hitchcock) | A masterclass in suspense and psychological terror. |
| 1978 | **The Shining** (dir. Stanley Kubrick) | Atmospheric dread, iconic imagery, and a chilling performance by Jack Nicholson. |
| 1984 | **The Thing** (dir. John Carpenter) | A tense, claustrophobic alien invasion with groundbreaking practical effects. |
| 1991 | **The Silence of the Lambs** (dir. Jonathan Demme) | A psychological thriller that blends horror with crime‑procedural intrigue. |
| 1999 | **The Blair Witch Project** (dir. Daniel Myrick & Eduardo Sánchez) | Pioneered the found‑footage style; its realism amplifies the fear. |
| 2002 | **28 Days Later** (dir. Danny Boyle) | Fast‑moving zombie outbreak with a gritty, post‑apocalyptic vibe. |
| 2004 | **Saw** (dir. James Wan) | Dark, inventive traps that test morality and survival instincts. |
| 2007 | **Paranormal Activity** (dir. Oren Peli) | Low‑budget found‑footage that still delivers genuine chills. |
| 2010 | **The Conjuring** (dir. James Wan) | A modern supernatural thriller grounded in real‑life paranormal investigations. |
| 2012 | **The Cabin in the Woods** (dir. Drew Goddard) | A meta‑take on horror tropes that’s both funny and genuinely scary. |
| 2014 | **It Follows** (dir. David Robert Mitchell) | A fresh take on the “invisible threat” concept with a haunting soundtrack. |
| 2015 | **The Witch** (dir. Robert Eggers) | A slow‑burn, period‑accurate horror that builds dread through atmosphere. |
| 2017 | **Get Out** (dir. Jordan Peele) | A socially conscious horror that blends satire with genuine terror. |
| 2018 | **A Quiet Place** (dir. John Krasinski) | Tension built around silence; a unique premise that keeps you on edge. |
| 2019 | **Midsommar** (dir. Ari Aster) | Daylight horror that turns a pastoral festival into a nightmare. |
| 2020 | **The Invisible Man** (dir. Leigh Whannell) | A modern retelling of a classic tale with strong feminist undertones. |
| 2021 | **Candyman** (dir. Nia DaCosta) | A contemporary reimagining of a horror legend with striking visuals. |
| 2022 | **The Black Phone** (dir. Scott Derrickson) | A supernatural thriller that mixes creepy folklore with a gripping narrative. |
| 2023 | **M3GAN** (dir. Gerard Johnstone) | A horror‑comedy about a murderous AI doll that’s both unsettling and oddly funny. |

Feel free to pick based on your preferred sub‑genre—psychological, supernatural, slasher, or found‑footage—and enjoy the chills!
